Much of analysis builds functions as limits: ex as a power series, sin⁡x as a Taylor series, the Weierstrass function of post 03 as a sum of cosines, solutions of differential equations as limits of approximations. The question is always the same: which properties survive the limit? Continuity, integrals and derivatives can all be lost under the obvious "point by point" notion of convergence. This post introduces the stronger notion that repairs most of this, uniform convergence, proves exactly what it preserves (continuity and integrals) and what it does not (derivatives, without an extra hypothesis), and then applies it to power series: radius of convergence, term-by-term calculus, Abel's theorem, and the difference between a Taylor series and the function it came from. It closes the core course with the Weierstrass approximation theorem and a map of where analysis goes next.
Series map: 00 The Real Numbers & Completeness → 01 Sequences & Series → 02 Topology of ℝ & Continuity → 03 Differentiation & Taylor's Theorem → 04 The Riemann Integral → 05 Uniform Convergence & Power Series (this post).

Sequence of functions — functions fn:A→R, n=1,2,…, all on the same domain A⊆R.
Pointwise convergence — fn→f pointwise on A if for each fixed x∈A, the number sequence fn(x) converges to f(x). In quantifiers: for every x∈A and every ε>0 there is N (which may depend on both x and ε) with ∣fn(x)−f(x)∣<ε for n≥N.
Uniform convergence — fn→f uniformly on A if for every ε>0 there is N (depending on ε only) with ∣fn(x)−f(x)∣<ε for all n≥N and all x∈A.
Sup norm — for a bounded g:A→R, ∥g∥∞=sup⁡x∈A∣g(x)∣.
Epsilon-tube — the band of width ε on each side of the graph of f. Uniform convergence says: from some N on, the whole graph of every fn lies inside the tube.
The only difference between the two definitions is the order of "there is N" and "for all x". Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence; the converse fails.
Sup-norm test. fn→f uniformly on A if and only if ∥fn−f∥∞→0 (where ∥fn−f∥∞ is finite for large n). This is the definition rewritten: "∣fn(x)−f(x)∣<ε for all x" gives sup⁡≤ε, and sup⁡<ε gives it for all x.

Let fn(x)=xn on [0,1]. For 0≤x<1, xn→0 (post 01); at x=1, 1n=1. So the pointwise limit is
f(x)={00≤x<1,1x=1.
Every fn is continuous, and the limit is not. The convergence is not uniform: the point xn=(1/2)1/n lies in [0,1) and fn(xn)−f(xn)=12, so ∥fn−f∥∞≥12 for every n (in fact the sup over [0,1) is 1). The "bad point" slides towards 1:
n · 1 · 2 · 5 · 10 · 50
xn=(1/2)1/n · 0.5 · 0.7071 · 0.8706 · 0.9330 · 0.9862
For each fixed x<1 you eventually get close to 0, but no single N works for all x at once.
On a smaller domain the problem disappears. On [0,12], ∥xn−0∥∞=(12)n→0, so xn→0 uniformly on [0,12], and indeed on [0,r] for any r<1.
Damping the bad point. Multiply by (1−x): kn(x)=xn(1−x) on [0,1]. The pointwise limit is 0 everywhere (including x=1, where kn(1)=0). Setting kn′(x)=xn−1(n−(n+1)x)=0 gives the maximum at x=nn+1, so
∥kn∥∞=(nn+1)n1n+1<1n+1→0.
So kn→0 uniformly on all of [0,1]. For example, ∥k10∥∞=10101111≈0.0350. The factor (1−x) kills the values near 1 exactly where xn misbehaved.

Let gn(x)=x2+1/n2 on R. With h=1/n,
0≤x2+h2−∣x∣=h2x2+h2+∣x∣≤h2h=h,
with equality at x=0. So ∥gn−∣x∣∥∞=1n→0: uniform convergence to ∣x∣ on all of R. With ε=0.25, every gn with n≥5 lies inside the ε-tube around ∣x∣ (its largest error is 15=0.2), while g2 (error 0.5) does not.
Every gn is smooth, and the limit ∣x∣ has a corner. Uniform convergence preserved continuity but not differentiability. Chapter 2 explains both facts.

Theorem. A sequence (fn) converges uniformly on A if and only if for every ε>0 there is N with
∣fn(x)−fm(x)∣<εfor all m,n≥N and all x∈A.
Proof. (⇒) If ∣fn−f∣<ε/2 everywhere for n≥N, then ∣fn−fm∣≤∣fn−f∣+∣f−fm∣<ε.
(⇐) For each fixed x, (fn(x)) is a Cauchy sequence of reals, so it converges (completeness, post 01); call the limit f(x). Given ε, take N from the hypothesis. For n≥N and any x, let m→∞ in ∣fn(x)−fm(x)∣<ε to get ∣fn(x)−f(x)∣≤ε. The same N works for every x, so the convergence is uniform. ■
The value of the criterion: it proves uniform convergence without knowing the limit in advance. The M-test in Chapter 3 is built on it.

Theorem. If each fn is continuous at c∈A and fn→f uniformly on A, then f is continuous at c.
Proof (the ε/3 argument). Let ε>0. Choose N with ∣fN(x)−f(x)∣<ε/3 for all x∈A. Since fN is continuous at c, choose δ with ∣fN(x)−fN(c)∣<ε/3 for ∣x−c∣<δ. Then for such x,
∣f(x)−f(c)∣≤∣f(x)−fN(x)∣+∣fN(x)−fN(c)∣+∣fN(c)−f(c)∣<ε3+ε3+ε3=ε.■
The first and third terms need the same N at two different points, x and c. That is exactly what uniformity supplies and pointwise convergence does not. The theorem also gives a quick proof that xn does not converge uniformly on [0,1]: the limit is discontinuous.
A partial converse (Dini's theorem). If K is compact, each fn is continuous on K, fn(x)≥fn+1(x) for all x and n, and fn→f pointwise with f continuous, then the convergence is uniform. (Rudin, Theorem 7.13.) All four hypotheses are needed; xn on [0,1] fails only "the limit is continuous".

Theorem. If each fn is Riemann integrable on [a,b] and fn→f uniformly on [a,b], then f is integrable and
∫abf=lim⁡n→∞∫abfn.
Proof. Let εn=∥fn−f∥∞, which tends to 0. Then fn−εn≤f≤fn+εn on [a,b] (so f is bounded). Upper and lower sums respect these inequalities, so the upper and lower integrals of f (post 04) satisfy
∫abfn−εn(b−a)≤∫ab‾f≤∫ab‾f≤∫abfn+εn(b−a).
The gap between the upper and lower integrals is at most 2εn(b−a)→0, so they are equal and f is integrable. The same inequalities give ∣∫abf−∫abfn∣≤εn(b−a)→0. ■
Pointwise convergence is not enough. Let fn(x)=nx(1−x2)n on [0,1]. For 0<x<1, fn(x)→0 (a geometric factor beats the factor n), and fn(0)=fn(1)=0. So fn→0 pointwise. But
∫01nx(1−x2)n dx=[−n2(n+1)(1−x2)n+1]01=n2(n+1)→12≠0=∫010 dx.
The convergence is far from uniform: the maximum of fn, at x=1/2n+1, grows without bound (about 1.34 for n=10 and 4.28 for n=100). A travelling spike keeps area ≈12 while its base shrinks.

Uniform convergence of fn says nothing about fn′. Two warnings:
gn(x)=x2+1/n2→∣x∣ uniformly (Chapter 1): smooth functions, non-differentiable limit.
hn(x)=sin⁡(n2x)n→0 uniformly on R (the sup norm is 1n), but hn′(x)=ncos⁡(n2x), and hn′(0)=n→∞. The derivatives do not converge to the derivative of the limit, which is 0.
The fix is to assume uniform convergence of the derivatives.
Theorem (limits of derivatives). Let each fn be differentiable on [a,b]. Suppose (fn(x0)) converges for some x0∈[a,b], and (fn′) converges uniformly on [a,b]. Then (fn) converges uniformly on [a,b] to a function f, and f′(x)=lim⁡n→∞fn′(x) for every x∈[a,b]. (Rudin, Theorem 7.17.)
Idea of proof (with the extra assumption that each fn′ is continuous). By FTC 2 (post 04), fn(x)=fn(x0)+∫x0xfn′. The integrals converge uniformly by the integral theorem above, so fn→f(x)=f(x0)+∫x0xg with g=lim⁡fn′, which is continuous as a uniform limit. FTC 1 gives f′=g. The general proof uses the Mean Value Theorem instead of integrals.
Watch out: "uniformly" in this theorem is about the derivatives. Uniform convergence of fn alone never licenses swapping lim⁡ and ddx.

A series of functions ∑k=1∞uk(x) converges pointwise or uniformly on A when its partial sums Sn(x)=∑k=1nuk(x) do. The three theorems of Chapter 2 become:
If the series converges uniformly on the interval and · then
each uk is continuous · the sum is continuous
each uk is integrable on [a,b] · ∫∑uk=∑∫uk (integrate term by term)
each uk is differentiable, ∑uk′ converges uniformly, ∑uk(x0) converges · (∑uk)′=∑uk′ (differentiate term by term)
Theorem (Weierstrass M-test). Suppose ∣uk(x)∣≤Mk for all x∈A and all k, and ∑Mk converges. Then ∑uk converges uniformly (and absolutely) on A.
Proof. For n>m and every x∈A,
∣Sn(x)−Sm(x)∣=∣∑k=m+1nuk(x)∣≤∑k=m+1nMk.
The right side does not depend on x, and it is small for large m because ∑Mk converges (Cauchy criterion for number series, post 01). So the partial sums satisfy the uniform Cauchy criterion of Chapter 1. ■
Worked example. F(x)=∑k=1∞sin⁡(kx)k2. Take Mk=1k2; ∑1k2 converges (its value is π26). So the series converges uniformly on R and F is continuous. Term-by-term differentiation would give ∑cos⁡(kx)k, which diverges at x=0 (harmonic series). So the M-test gives continuity, and says nothing about differentiability.
The same test proves the continuity of the Weierstrass function in post 03: ∣ancos⁡(bnπx)∣≤an with ∑an a convergent geometric series.
Common pitfall: the M-test is sufficient, not necessary. ∑k≥1(−1)k+1k (constant functions) converges uniformly, trivially, but no summable Mk≥1k exists.

Power series about x0 — a series ∑k=0∞ak(x−x0)k with real coefficients ak. Below, x0=0 for simplicity.
Radius of convergence — the number R∈[0,∞] such that the series converges absolutely for ∣x∣<R and diverges for ∣x∣>R. At x=±R anything can happen.
Limit superior — lim sup⁡kbk=lim⁡n→∞sup⁡k≥nbk, which always exists in [−∞,∞] (monotone convergence, post 01).

Theorem (Cauchy–Hadamard). Let β=lim sup⁡k→∞∣ak∣1/k. Then the radius of convergence is R=1/β (with R=∞ if β=0 and R=0 if β=∞).
Proof. Apply the root test (post 01) to ∑∣akxk∣: lim sup⁡∣akxk∣1/k=β∣x∣. If β∣x∣<1 the series converges absolutely; if β∣x∣>1 the terms do not tend to 0, so it diverges. ■
Ratio formula. If lim⁡∣akak+1∣ exists (in [0,∞]), it equals R. When it applies it is easier; when it does not, the root formula still works.
Series · R · At x=R · At x=−R
∑xk · 1 · diverges · diverges
∑xk/k (from k=1) · 1 · diverges (harmonic) · converges (alternating)
∑xk/k2 (from k=1) · 1 · converges · converges
∑xk/k! · ∞ · — · —
∑k! xk · 0 · — · —
The first three show that all endpoint behaviours occur with the same radius.
When the ratio test fails. Let ak=2k for even k and ak=1 for odd k. The ratios ∣ak/ak+1∣ alternate between values tending to 0 and to ∞, so they have no limit. But ∣ak∣1/k is 2 for even k and 1 for odd k, so lim sup⁡=2 and R=12.

Theorem. If 0<r<R, the power series converges uniformly on [−r,r]. Consequently it converges uniformly on every compact subset of (−R,R), and its sum is continuous on (−R,R).
Proof. Since r<R, the series converges absolutely at x=r, so ∑∣ak∣rk converges. On [−r,r], ∣akxk∣≤∣ak∣rk=Mk. Apply the M-test. A compact K⊂(−R,R) is closed and bounded, so its max of ∣x∣ is some r<R and K⊆[−r,r]. Every x∈(−R,R) lies in some [−r,r], and continuity is local. ■
Watch out: the convergence need not be uniform on the whole open interval. For ∑xk on (−1,1) the tail after xn is ∑k>nxk=xn+11−x, which is unbounded as x→1− for every n.

Theorem. Let f(x)=∑k=0∞akxk with radius R>0. Then on (−R,R):
f′(x)=∑k=1∞k akxk−1,∫0xf(t) dt=∑k=0∞akk+1xk+1,
and both new series also have radius R. Hence f is infinitely differentiable on (−R,R), and ak=f(k)(0)k!: a power series is the Taylor series of its own sum.
Proof sketch. Since k1/k→1, lim sup⁡(k∣ak∣)1/k=lim sup⁡∣ak∣1/k, so the differentiated series has the same radius (similarly for the integrated one). On any [−r,r] with r<R the differentiated series converges uniformly, so the derivative theorem (Chapter 2) applies. Integration follows from the integral theorem. Repeating gives all derivatives, and evaluating the k-th derivative at 0 leaves only k! ak. ■
Worked example 1. From 11−x=∑k≥0xk on (−1,1), differentiate: 1(1−x)2=∑k≥1kxk−1. Multiply by x and put x=12:
∑k=1∞k2k=1/2(1−1/2)2=2.
Worked example 2. From 11+t=∑k≥0(−1)ktk on (−1,1), integrate from 0 to x:
ln⁡(1+x)=x−x22+x33−⋯=∑k=1∞(−1)k+1kxk,∣x∣<1.
Worked example 3. E(x)=∑k≥0xkk! has R=∞. Differentiating term by term gives E′=E, with E(0)=1. So E(x)=ex (the function E(x)e−x has zero derivative, hence is constant, by post 03).

The formula for ln⁡(1+x) was proved for ∣x∣<1. At x=1 the series 1−12+13−… converges (alternating series test, post 01), but does it converge to ln⁡2?
Theorem (Abel). Suppose ∑k=0∞ak converges. Then f(x)=∑akxk converges for ∣x∣<1 and
lim⁡x→1−f(x)=∑k=0∞ak.
Proof. Let s=∑ak. Replacing a0 by a0−s changes f by the constant −s and makes the sum 0, so assume s=0. Let sn=a0+⋯+an; then sn→0, so (sn) is bounded and ∑skxk converges for ∣x∣<1. Summation by parts (ak=sk−sk−1) gives, for 0<x<1,
f(x)=∑k=0∞akxk=(1−x)∑k=0∞skxk.
Given ε>0, choose N with ∣sk∣<ε for k>N. Then
∣f(x)∣≤(1−x)∑k=0N∣sk∣+ε(1−x)∑k>Nxk≤(1−x)∑k=0N∣sk∣+ε.
The first term tends to 0 as x→1−, so ∣f(x)∣<2ε for x close enough to 1. Hence f(x)→0=s. ■
Apply it to ak=(−1)k+1k: the left side is lim⁡x→1−ln⁡(1+x)=ln⁡2 by continuity of ln⁡. So
1−12+13−14+⋯=ln⁡2≈0.693147.
The same argument with arctan⁡x=∑k≥0(−1)kx2k+12k+1 gives 1−13+15−⋯=π4. (These series converge slowly: the first 10 terms of the ln⁡2 series sum to 0.6456.)
Common pitfall: Abel's theorem needs the series at x=1 to converge. For ak=(−1)k, f(x)=11+x→12 as x→1−, but ∑(−1)k diverges; the limit 12 is not a sum in the ordinary sense.

For a C∞ function f, the Taylor series at 0 is ∑f(k)(0)k!xk. Two things can go wrong:
The series can have radius 0 (there are C∞ functions like this).
The series can converge, to a different function.
Case 2 is the function of post 03: f(x)=e−1/x2 with f(0)=0. All derivatives at 0 vanish, so its Taylor series is 0+0x+0x2+…, with radius ∞ and sum 0. It equals f only at x=0.
The link to Taylor's theorem is the remainder: the Taylor series of f converges to f(x) exactly when Rn(x)→0. For ex at any x, the Lagrange remainder satisfies ∣Rn(x)∣≤e∣x∣∣x∣n+1(n+1)!→0, so ex equals its Taylor series everywhere. A function is real analytic at x0 when it equals a convergent power series on some interval around x0. By the term-by-term theorem, such a power series must be the Taylor series. So: analytic ⇒ C∞, but not conversely.

Not every continuous function is a power series, but every continuous function is uniformly close to a polynomial.
Theorem (Weierstrass, 1885). Let f be continuous on [a,b]. For every ε>0 there is a polynomial p with ∣f(x)−p(x)∣<ε for all x∈[a,b].
Bernstein's constructive proof (idea). On [0,1], define
Bnf(x)=∑k=0nf ⁣(kn)(nk)xk(1−x)n−k.
The weights (nk)xk(1−x)n−k are the binomial probabilities of k successes in n trials with success probability x. They add up to 1 and concentrate near k/n≈x as n grows, so Bnf(x) is a weighted average of values of f near x. Uniform continuity of f (post 02) turns this into ∥Bnf−f∥∞→0.
Worked example. For f(x)=x2 a direct computation gives
Bnf(x)=x2+x(1−x)n,
so the error is x(1−x)n, largest at x=12, and ∥Bnf−f∥∞=14n. An error of at most 0.01 needs n≥25. The convergence is uniform but slow; Bernstein polynomials are valued for their shape-preserving properties (they are the basis of Bézier curves), not their speed.
Compare with the Weierstrass function of post 03: a continuous, nowhere-differentiable function can still be approximated uniformly, to any accuracy, by polynomials, which are as smooth as functions get. Uniform limits keep continuity and lose everything finer.

Metric spaces. Uniform convergence is convergence in the metric d(f,g)=∥f−g∥∞ on C[a,b]. Chapter 1's Cauchy criterion, together with the continuity theorem of Chapter 2, says this space is complete, and Weierstrass says polynomials are dense in it. The same words (complete, dense, compact) from posts 00–02 now describe spaces of functions.
Lebesgue integration. The spike example nx(1−x2)n shows that pointwise limits and integrals do not commute in general. Lebesgue's theory says exactly when they do (monotone and dominated convergence), without asking for uniformity.
Fourier series. Replacing powers xk by cos⁡(kx) and sin⁡(kx) gives Fourier series. Their convergence is subtler than for power series: the Fourier series of a discontinuous square wave converges pointwise at every point but never uniformly, which ties back to the continuity theorem of Chapter 2.

Exercise 1. Show that fn(x)=xn converges uniformly on [0,1] but not on R.
Solution
The pointwise limit is 0. On [0,1], ∥fn∥∞=1n→0: uniform. On R, sup⁡x∣x/n∣=∞ for every n (take x=n to get fn(n)=1): not uniform.
Exercise 2. Let fn(x)=xn. Prove that fn→0 uniformly on [0,r] for each r<1, and explain in one line why it cannot be uniform on [0,1) even though the limit 0 is continuous there.
Solution
On [0,r], ∥xn∥∞=rn→0. On [0,1), the points xn=(1/2)1/n give xnn=12, so sup⁡[0,1)xn≥12 for every n. (The continuity theorem only says a discontinuous limit rules out uniformity; a continuous limit does not guarantee it.)
Exercise 3. Use the M-test to show that ∑k=1∞xkk2 converges uniformly on [−1,1]. Is its sum continuous at x=1?
Solution
For ∣x∣≤1, ∣xkk2∣≤1k2=Mk, and ∑1k2 converges. So the series converges uniformly on [−1,1] and the sum is continuous there, including at the endpoint x=1 (one-sided).
Exercise 4. Find the radius of convergence of ∑k≥1k23kxk and of ∑k≥0(2k)!(k!)2xk.
Solution
First: ∣ak∣1/k=k2/k3→13, so R=3. Second, by the ratio formula: ak+1ak=(2k+2)(2k+1)(k+1)2→4, so R=14.
Exercise 5. Compute ∑k≥1k3k using term-by-term differentiation.
Solution
From ∑k≥1kxk=x(1−x)2 for ∣x∣<1, put x=13: 1/3(2/3)2=1/34/9=34.

∫01fn=n2(n+1), so for n=10 it

Exercise 6. For fn(x)=nx(1−x2)n on [0,1], compute ∫01fn for n=10 and explain why this does not contradict the integral theorem.
Solution
∫01fn=n2(n+1), so for n=10 it is 1022=511≈0.4545. The pointwise limit is 0 with integral 0. No contradiction: the convergence is not uniform (the maximum of f10 is about 1.34 and the maxima grow without bound), so the theorem does not apply.
Exercise 7. Show that the Bernstein polynomial Bnf of f(x)=x is x itself for every n.
Solution
Bnf(x)=∑k=0nkn(nk)xk(1−x)n−k. This is 1n times the mean of a binomial distribution with n trials and success probability x, which is nx. So Bnf(x)=x. (Bernstein polynomials reproduce linear functions exactly; the first error appears for x2.)
